entries.example: Take the arrow for the vector (2, 3): it moves 2 right and 3 up. Draw exactly the same arrow again starting at a new start point - still 2 right and 3 up - and it is the same vector: sliding it did not change its magnitude sqrt(13) or its direction. Only a position vector would change, because a position vector is pinned to the origin.
entries.meaning: A quantity with both magnitude and direction, pictured as an arrow: the arrow for (2, 3) moves 2 right and 3 up.

entries.example: A vector has size and direction: the arrow moves 2 right and 3 up, its column vector records 2 over 3, and the length of the arrow is its magnitude.
entries.meaning: The length of the vector arrow: for (x, y) it is sqrt(x^2 + y^2) by Pythagoras, so |(2, 3)| = sqrt(13).

entries.example: A vector has size and direction: the arrow moves 2 right and 3 up, its column vector records 2 over 3, and the length of the arrow is its magnitude.
entries.meaning: The record of a vector as its components stacked in a column: the top entry is the right move and the bottom entry is the up move, as in 2 over 3.

entries.example: The dot product measures the shadow: drop a perpendicular from the tip of b onto a, and the projection is measured by a . b = |a||b| cos theta.
entries.meaning: The scalar a . b = |a||b| cos theta, computed component by component; it measures how much of b points along a, and it is zero exactly when the vectors are perpendicular.

entries.example: A common mistake: moving a vector changes it: sliding a free vector to a new start point leaves it unchanged - only position vectors are pinned to the origin.
entries.meaning: The vector of a point measured from the origin: it is pinned to the origin, so moving the point changes its position vector.

entries.example: Lines and planes from a point and directions: one point plus one direction draws a line, r = a + lambda b; a plane needs two directions and its normal stands perpendicular to the whole surface.
entries.meaning: A free vector that gives the direction of a line or plane edge: the same arrow drawn anywhere is the same direction vector, as in r = a + lambda b.
